question: A 6-week-old infant is brought to clinic with noisy inspiratory breathing present since birth. The stridor is worse when the baby is supine, crying, or feeding, and improves when prone. The infant is gaining weight adequately, has no fever, and the cry is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Epiglottitis is an acute bacterial infection occurring in older unvaccinated children (classically 2–7 years), presenting with rapid onset fever, drooling, and toxic appearance. It does not present as a chronic, intermittent stridor from birth in a thriving, afebrile 6-week-old.

Correct. Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of chronic stridor in infants and the most common laryngeal anomaly. Floppy supraglottic structures (arytenoids and aryepiglottic folds) collapse inward on inspiration, producing characteristic inspiratory stridor that worsens when supine, feeding, or crying, and improves when prone. Onset from birth, normal cry, and adequate weight gain all support the diagnosis. Over 90% resolve spontaneously by 18–24 months.

Subglottic stenosis produces biphasic stridor and is less positional than laryngomalacia. It can be congenital but is more commonly acquired after prolonged intubation. The purely inspiratory, position-dependent stridor from birth in a thriving infant with a normal cry is more consistent with laryngomalacia.

A vascular ring (aberrant great vessel compressing the trachea) typically produces biphasic stridor and is frequently associated with dysphagia (posterior oesophageal compression). Position-dependent purely inspiratory stridor improving when prone is the hallmark of laryngomalacia, not vascular ring.

overallFeedback.feedback: The most common cause of congenital/chronic stridor in infants from birth with position-dependent worsening and normal weight gain is laryngomalacia. Epiglottitis is acute in older children; subglottic stenosis is biphasic; vascular ring involves dysphagia and biphasic stridor.

Correct. Laryngomalacia is the most common cause of chronic infantile stridor: onset from birth, inspiratory stridor worsening supine/feeding/crying, improving prone, normal cry and weight gain. It resolves spontaneously in over 90% by 18–24 months.
